title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text: NorthPoint built its own logistic regression, the bank’s incident-association model, from its panel. Its headline: vendors without a current SOC 2 Type II report have about twice the odds of an incident (odds ratio 2.04, vendor-clustered 95% interval 1.48 to 2.82). That finding now supports a contract policy. How small a change makes it disappear?

title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text: NorthPoint built its own logistic regression, the bank’s incident-association model, from its panel. Its headline: vendors without a current SOC 2 Type II report have about twice the odds of an incident (odds ratio 2.04, vendor-clustered 95% interval 1.48 to 2.82). That finding now supports a contract policy. How small a change makes it disappear?

title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text:
Method in brief
Pre-registered definition of a “kill”: the no-SOC-2 coefficient loses statistical significance at the 5% level using vendor-clustered standard errors (sandwich::vcovCL, Wald z). Ordinary standard errors ignore within-vendor dependence and may overstate precision.
A specification curve re-estimates the odds ratio across 16 logit models (so every estimate is an odds ratio): include or omit vendor size, prior incidents and financial health, with or without trimming the slowest 1% of patch latencies. A greedy deletion search then removes, one at a time, the incident rows that most support the estimate, from the analysis dataset only; recorded lagged history is kept. Both are bounded searches, not proofs of what is smallest.
The falsifyr package supplies the refits and a supplementary within-model attack run.1

title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text:
Findings


Show the code
cv$label <- ifelse(cv$vendor_size, "Vendor size included", "Vendor size omitted")
ggplot(cv, aes(rank, or, colour = label)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = fr$true_or, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), size = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(okabe_ito[c("blue", "vermillion")])) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.8, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3), labels = c("0.8", "1", "1.25", "1.5", "2", "3")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Specification (ordered by odds ratio)",
       y = "Odds ratio for no SOC 2 (log scale)", colour = NULL)








Figure 1: No-SOC-2 odds ratio across 16 logit specifications, ordered by size, with 95% vendor-clustered intervals. Dashed line: data-generating conditional OR, 1.25.






How to read the plot. Each dot is one reasonable way of building the model; height is the estimated increase in the odds of an incident for vendors without SOC 2, and 1 means no effect. The vertical line is the plausible range. The dashed line is the generator’s conditional odds ratio, known because the data are simulated.
What the plot tells you. The dots form two groups, split by one decision: vendor size. Larger vendors are more likely to hold SOC 2 and are safer, so leaving size out credits SOC 2 with that safety. Closeness to 1.25 does not prove a causal model has been recovered.

All 8 specifications without vendor size are significant (odds ratios 2.04 to 2.43); none of the 8 that include it is (1.28 to 1.36). Adding vendor size alone takes the estimate to 1.28 (interval 0.90 to 1.82, p = 0.163) with no data removed. This concerns the association; it does not show that SOC 2 has no effect.


Show the code
dp <- fr$deletion_path
ggplot(dp, aes(step, p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_line(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], size = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(step = 0, p = ps$p), shape = 18, size = 5,
             colour = okabe_ito[["vermillion"]]) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Incident vendor-months deleted (greedy search)",
       y = "Clustered p-value (log scale)")








Figure 2: Greedy deletion search: clustered p-value as supportive incident rows are deleted. The diamond is the size-adjusted model with nothing deleted.






How to read the plot. The blue line removes, one at a time, incidents at vendors without SOC 2 that most support the finding, and tracks how convincing the result stays. Higher means weaker evidence; above the dashed line it is no longer statistically significant. The diamond is the size-adjusted result, with no rows removed.
What the plot tells you. This is an adversarial stress test, not data cleaning. The two routes to the 5% line are different kinds of distance, so they should not be compared by counting.

The search found a successful perturbation, within its budget of 80 deletions, at 29 deleted rows: 0.20% of all 14,400 rows, 13.9% of all 209 incidents and 20.6% of the 141 eligible supportive incidents. A greedy search gives an upper bound on the smallest such change, and post-search p-values are diagnostics, not fresh tests. falsifyr found no kill in its run (verdict resilient), which is not proof of robustness.
Seed sensitivity. Each seed generates a different synthetic dataset, so this is a Monte Carlo repeatability check, not a perturbation of the bank’s data. We re-ran the generator for seeds 1 to 40, with the same clustered baseline. The omitted-size odds ratio ranged from 1.30 to 2.77 (median 2.01), significant in 38 of 40 runs. With size included it ranged from 0.84 to 1.78 (median 1.29), significant in 9. These counts are descriptive and imprecise. Seed 34 was chosen during development because it illustrates the intended patterns so its p-values are not an unbiased experiment. The upward bias from omitting size is repeatable; the exact “2×” is not.

title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text:
So what?
The “2× odds” headline reflects confounding in this simulator, not a robust effect of SOC 2: the size-adjusted estimate is 1.28 (0.90 to 1.82), which is also compatible with a sizeable effect. The bank’s own model was built to describe associations, then reused to support a contract policy. The April 17, 2026 interagency Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) flags use beyond a model’s intended purpose (§IV, Model Use), and describes effective challenge (§III) and testing with alternative assumptions (§IV). The challenge here was one added variable. This is partial validation too; even a robust association would not be causal.


Show the code
score <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Calibration", "Forecast dominance", "Fragility"),
  Question = c("Honest probabilities?", "Beats a simple model?", "Robust headline?"),
  `Measured result` = c(
    sprintf("Raw top group predicted %s, observed %s. Isotonic overlay changes Brier by %s (%s to %s); gains small and unclear.",
            pct(raw_top$predicted), pct(raw_top$observed), sgn(brier_chg), sgn(cm$diff_low), sgn(cm$diff_high)),
    sprintf("MSE %s lower than the 12-month average; DM p = %s (n = 18): no detectable advantage.",
            pct(1 - full$mse_vs / full$mse_naive, 0), pval(full$dm_p)),
    sprintf("Odds ratio %s becomes %s (p = %s) when vendor size is added; one added variable removes significance.",
            num(b$or), num(ps$or), num(ps$p))),
  `Suggested response` = c(
    "Do not approve the tested overlay for routine use yet; investigate, keep the existing process under documented controls, validate any replacement on later outcomes.",
    "Closer monitoring; raise with vendor; ask for development evidence; keep contingency plan.",
    "Limit use: do not use this association alone to infer the effect of requiring SOC 2; document the exception."),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(score)




Table 1: Series scorecard: measured results at NorthPoint, and responses in the guidance’s vocabulary (measured result and decision kept separate).












Test
Question
Measured result
Suggested response




Calibration
Honest probabilities?
Raw top group predicted 10.8%, observed 6.9%. Isotonic overlay changes Brier by −0.00026 (−0.00064 to 0.00004); gains small and unclear.
Do not approve the tested overlay for routine use yet; investigate, keep the existing process under documented controls, validate any replacement on later outcomes.


Forecast dominance
Beats a simple model?
MSE 22% lower than the 12-month average; DM p = 0.235 (n = 18): no detectable advantage.
Closer monitoring; raise with vendor; ask for development evidence; keep contingency plan.


Fragility
Robust headline?
Odds ratio 2.04 becomes 1.28 (p = 0.16) when vendor size is added; one added variable removes significance.
Limit use: do not use this association alone to infer the effect of requiring SOC 2; document the exception.









How to read the table. One row per question: what we measured at NorthPoint, and the action sound practice suggests, in the guidance’s vocabulary. An overlay adjusts a model’s output without changing the model; limits on use restrict what a result may be used for.
What the table tells you. None of the three tests found anything clean, and none, alone, argues for scrapping VendorScore. The weakest item is the bank’s own finding.

title: Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?
text:
Actionable Insights
Sound practice suggests documenting the SOC 2 finding as an exception (§VI) and analysing its new use before relying on it (§IV). Do not use this association alone to infer the effect of requiring SOC 2: contract requirements need business, legal and control evidence. The guidance does not prescribe this.

Its configured routine did not evaluate the added-control specification under our vendor-clustered inference rule, so we implemented that check separately.↩︎

title: Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?
text: When VendorScore says a vendor has a 10% chance of an incident, do incidents happen about 10% of the time? RiskMetric Systems asserts that its scores are “well-calibrated.” NorthPoint cannot inspect the model, but it can compare the scores with what happened, and it can test whether a recalibration overlay would help.

title: Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?
text: When VendorScore says a vendor has a 10% chance of an incident, do incidents happen about 10% of the time? RiskMetric Systems asserts that its scores are “well-calibrated.” NorthPoint cannot inspect the model, but it can compare the scores with what happened, and it can test whether a recalibration overlay would help.

title: Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?
text:
Method in brief
VendorScore trained on months 1 to 30 (the vendor’s business). We fitted the overlay on months 31 to 36 (1,800 vendor-months, 28 incidents), so the classifier had not trained on those rows. Every result below comes from months 37 to 48 (3,600 vendor-months, 75 incidents, 300 vendors), which nothing was fitted or selected on.
We fixed the methods before looking at that window: an isotonic overlay (a monotone curve, interpolated between fitted points), and a Platt overlay (a logistic curve on the logit of the score) as secondary. Both come from probcal.1 The Brier score measures overall probability error, so it reflects more than calibration. The expected calibration error (ECE) is the weighted average gap between score and outcome across ten score groups; it depends on how groups are formed, so we show equal-size and equal-width groups. Uncertainty comes from resampling whole vendor histories (1,000 draws), because the same vendors recur every month. Intervals condition on the fitted overlay and leave out overlay-fitting uncertainty.

title: Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?
text:
Findings


Show the code
rel2 <- rel[rel$score %in% c("Raw VendorScore", "Isotonic overlay"), ]
rel2$score <- factor(rel2$score, levels = c("Raw VendorScore", "Isotonic overlay"))
brk <- c(0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10)
ggplot(rel2, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high, colour = score), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = score), size = 2.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = true_mean), shape = 5, colour = "grey25", size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~score) +
  scale_x_sqrt(breaks = brk, labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 0.12)) +
  scale_y_sqrt(breaks = brk, labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 0.12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(okabe_ito[c("vermillion", "blue")]), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Average predicted probability (square-root scale)",
       y = "Observed incident rate (square-root scale)")








Figure 1: Reliability diagram, months 37–48. Filled points: observed rate with vendor-clustered 95% intervals. Open diamonds: mean true probability in the group.






How to read the plot. Each dot groups vendor-months with similar scores: left to right is the prediction, bottom to top is what happened. A dot on the grey diagonal means the model was right on average. The vertical line is a plausible range; the open diamond is the true average risk, known only because the data are simulated.
What the plot tells you. In the raw panel, the top group is the clearest miss. Only 75 incidents lie behind these dots, so single-group intervals are wide.

The raw top-scored group was told it faced 10.8%; 6.9% had an incident (interval 4.5% to 9.5%), and its true average risk was 5.2%. The observed rate exceeded the score in 8 of 10 groups, mostly low-scored ones. These intervals are pointwise, so they do not amount to a global test. The isotonic overlay collapses tied scores into 5 distinct groups, not ten.


Show the code
tab <- data.frame(
  Scores = c("Raw VendorScore", "Isotonic overlay", "Platt overlay (logit scale)", "Observed"),
  Brier = c(sprintf("%.5f", pt[, "brier"]), "—"),
  `Brier change vs raw` = c("—", dif("Isotonic overlay", "brier"),
                            dif("Platt overlay (logit scale)", "brier"), "—"),
  `ECE, equal-size groups` = c(sprintf("%.4f", pt[, "ece_mass"]), "—"),
  `ECE, equal-width groups` = c(sprintf("%.4f", pt[, "ece_width"]), "—"),
  `Incidents per month` = c(sprintf("%.1f", pt[, "expected_per_month"]),
                            sprintf("%.1f", cal$observed_per_month)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, align = "lrrrrr")

How to read the table. Each row is a version of the scores; the last row is the actual count. Smaller Brier and ECE are better. The “change” column shows how each overlay moves Brier versus raw scores, with a plausible range in brackets. The last column is the incidents per month the scores imply.
What the table tells you. Both overlays lower Brier slightly, but the isotonic range includes zero and the Platt range only just excludes it. 3 of the 4 ECE changes have ranges that include zero. All three score versions imply fewer incidents (5.2 to 5.7 a month) than the 6.2 observed.

Overlay gains are small and statistically unclear. The raw count of 5.7 incidents a month is closest to what was observed. The true probabilities imply only 5.1, so some shortfall is chance. Changing vendor mix, thin calibration data and a six-month fitting window may all contribute; this exercise does not isolate them.


Show the code
mov <- cal$moves
mov$path <- factor(paste(mov$from, "→", mov$to),
                   levels = unique(paste(mov$from, "→", mov$to)[order(mov$move != "No change", mov$from)]))
ggplot(mov, aes(path, Freq, fill = move)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No change" = unname(okabe_ito["grey"]),
                               "Moves down" = unname(okabe_ito["blue"]),
                               "Moves up" = unname(okabe_ito["vermillion"]))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Risk band under raw → overlay scores", y = "Number of vendors", fill = NULL)








Figure 2: Vendors by risk band, raw versus isotonic-overlay scores (Low <1%, Medium 1–<3%, High ≥3% monthly probability; illustrative). A retrospective illustration.






How to read the plot. Vendors are put in Low, Medium or High risk bands using their average score over months 37 to 48. These bands are separate from the criticality tiers of vendors. Each bar counts vendors by band before and after the overlay.
What the plot tells you. 238 of 300 vendors keep their band and 62 move up; none move down. This shows the overlay’s decision impact, not that the new bands are right; averaging a whole window is a retrospective device, not a monitoring rule.

title: Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?
text:
So what?
The vendor’s calibration claim does not hold cleanly: the highest-risk group is overstated and the overlay evidence is thin. Outcomes analysis (§V) can support an overlay (§VII), but does not make one acceptable by itself. This one has not shown fitness for the use: Brier gains are small, ECE changes are mostly indistinguishable from zero, and no operational acceptance threshold was set in advance, so we do not invent one. This is a corrected retrospective demonstration, not a prospective validation, and only partial validation: it cannot say why the scores are miscalibrated or whether the proprietary method is conceptually sound.






NoteTechnical note: kernel calibration test (exploratory)



The kernel test in probcal::cal_test() on raw scores gives p = 0.023. It treats rows as independent although vendors recur monthly, so we do not rely on it.

title: Question 1: Are Its Probabilities Honest?
text:
Actionable Insights
Sound practice suggests not approving the tested overlay for routine use yet: investigate the shortfall, keep the existing process under documented controls, and validate any replacement on later outcomes against tolerances set in advance. Include a reliability diagram in every validation pack. The April 17, 2026 interagency Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) refers to the bank’s own established performance thresholds (§V).

title: Three Questions for Any Risk Model
text:
Your bank pays a vendor for a number. Every month, a model called VendorScore hands NorthPoint Bank a risk score for each of its 300 third-party vendors. Nobody at the bank can see the code, the training data, or the method. The scores arrive, and decisions follow.
How do you validate something you cannot open? This project shows how much can be learned from the scores and what happens afterwards, and where outside testing stops.

title: Three Questions for Any Risk Model
text:
Your bank pays a vendor for a number. Every month, a model called VendorScore hands NorthPoint Bank a risk score for each of its 300 third-party vendors. Nobody at the bank can see the code, the training data, or the method. The scores arrive, and decisions follow.
How do you validate something you cannot open? This project shows how much can be learned from the scores and what happens afterwards, and where outside testing stops.

title: Three Questions for Any Risk Model
text:
The three questions
The April 17, 2026 interagency Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) is explicitly non-prescriptive. We read it as describing sound practice, not rules. The three questions below are this project’s practical interpretation, not a regulator-prescribed checklist. Each works on any risk model.
Reading the § marks. § means “section.” Pages cite these parts of the guidance:

§III, overview of model risk: what makes a model risky, how much a model matters (materiality), and independent critical review (“effective challenge”).
§IV, development and use: how models are built and tested, and the risk of using a model for something it was not designed for.
§V, validation and monitoring: checking a model against real outcomes, watching it over time, and adjusting, recalibrating or rebuilding it if needed.
§VI, governance and controls: policies, roles and records, including documenting exceptions.
§VII, vendor products: applying the same discipline to bought models whose code and data the bank may never see.


Are its probabilities honest? When the model says 10%, do incidents happen about 10% of the time? This is calibration, tested with probcal (Page 2).
Does it beat a simple model? A sophisticated model should outperform a plain 12-month average, and keep doing so when conditions change. This is forecast dominance, tested with forecastdom (Page 3).
Would its headline finding survive a push? Some findings collapse under a small change of method or data. This is fragility, tested with falsifyr (Page 4).







Figure 1: Each test is tied to a question and to the decision it protects.




How to read the plot. Each of the three columns is one question. Reading down, each column shows the question, the test, and the decision it protects.
What the plot tells you. A model can pass one test and fail another, so one test alone leaves two decisions unprotected.







NoteMateriality box (illustrative ratings)



Judging how much validation a model deserves (guidance §III) looks at three things:

Inherent risk: high. VendorScore is opaque, its assumptions and data are hidden, and vendor incidents are rare events, which limits the data available to test it.
Exposure: broad. The score covers all 300 vendors in the portfolio.
Purpose: consequential. Scores inform monitoring intensity and contract terms.

Exposure and purpose together determine materiality, assessed alongside inherent risk. Illustrative conclusion: full validation is warranted.

title: Three Questions for Any Risk Model
text:
The case
NorthPoint Bank is a fictional regional bank with about $45 billion in assets. The guidance is expected to be most relevant to banks above $30 billion; some smaller banks may also find it relevant. Asset managers and fintechs fall outside its scope but can adopt similar practices voluntarily.
All pages share one synthetic dataset: 14,400 vendor-months (300 vendors over 48 months, January 2022 to December 2025), with 209 observed incidents, or 1.45% of vendor-months. Because the data are simulated, we know each vendor-month’s true incident probability, used only as a reference; the models never see it. Everything is reproducible from seed 34.
A fictional vendor, RiskMetric Systems, supplies VendorScore, trained on months 1 to 30. NorthPoint fits a recalibration overlay on months 31 to 36 and assesses it on months 37 to 48 (Page 2). Page 3 compares the raw scores with a benchmark over months 31 to 48, a period that includes a deterioration in vendors’ patching speed after month 36.

title: Three Questions for Any Risk Model
text:
The black-box problem
Guidance on vendor products (§VII) recognises that a bank may lack access to a vendor model’s inner workings. The vendor’s summary offers only “ensemble machine learning on proprietary threat intelligence,” an AUC of 0.81 “on vendor development data,” and the assertion that scores are “well-calibrated.”
The bank can evaluate how the scores perform on its own outcomes, for calibration and discrimination. It cannot reproduce the vendor’s development-data AUC or inspect the hidden development choices. Testing scores against outcomes is partial validation only: it cannot confirm that the proprietary model is conceptually sound. That depends on what the vendor discloses (§VII).

title: Three Questions for Any Risk Model
text:
How to read this project
Pages 2 to 4 share one structure: the question, the method in brief, the findings, what they mean for the bank, and one committee action phrased as “sound practice suggests…”. The expected findings were written as hypotheses before any analysis ran; where a result differs, the text reports the result. Code is folded by default. Page 4 closes with a scorecard of measured results; a final page covers reproducibility and limits.

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text: Does VendorScore forecast NorthPoint’s monthly incident total better than a plain 12-month rolling average of past counts, and does any advantage survive the deterioration in vendor patching after month 36? This tests one use of the model, aggregate monthly count forecasting. VendorScore may have other value, such as ranking vendors for attention, which this comparison does not price.

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text: Does VendorScore forecast NorthPoint’s monthly incident total better than a plain 12-month rolling average of past counts, and does any advantage survive the deterioration in vendor patching after month 36? This tests one use of the model, aggregate monthly count forecasting. VendorScore may have other value, such as ranking vendors for attention, which this comparison does not price.

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text:
Method in brief
Each forecast is made at the start of month t for the incidents that will occur during that month. VendorScore’s forecast is the sum of its 300 vendor scores. The benchmark is the mean of actual counts in months t − 12 to t − 1. We assume each month’s patch latency and financial health are observed at the start of that month; if they were end-of-month measures, this would be a contemporaneous assessment, not a one-step-ahead forecast. We use raw scores over months 31 to 48, so no fitting touches the target months.
We summarise accuracy with mean squared error (MSE, in squared incidents) and mean absolute error (MAE, in incidents). We test equal accuracy with the Diebold–Mariano test from forecastdom:1 a positive statistic means lower squared loss for VendorScore. We run it over months 31 to 48 and over months 37 to 48. With 18 and 12 observations the test has low power, and a small-sample correction does not cure a deliberately shifting environment, where loss patterns may not be stable.

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text:
Findings


Show the code
ggplot(long, aes(month, value, colour = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fc$shift_month, colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = subset(long, series == "Actual incidents"), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual incidents" = okabe_ito[["blue"]],
                                 "VendorScore forecast" = okabe_ito[["orange"]],
                                 "12-month average" = okabe_ito[["grey"]])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Actual incidents" = "solid",
                                   "VendorScore forecast" = "solid",
                                   "12-month average" = "longdash")) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Incidents per month (portfolio)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)








Figure 1: Monthly incident totals versus both forecasts, months 31–48. The vertical line marks month 36, the last month before patching latency drifts.






How to read the plot. Blue dots joined by a line are the actual incident counts across all 300 vendors. The orange line is VendorScore’s forecast and the grey dashed line is the 12-month average. The dotted line marks when patching began to slow.
What the plot tells you. Actual counts trend upward and swing widely. The 12-month average trails the trend and forecasts too low for most of the window, by 1.2 incidents a month on average. VendorScore’s average miss is 0.2. Both are conditional expected counts, not predictions of every fluctuation.



Show the code
ggplot(tst, aes(month, cum_diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fc$shift_month, colour = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_area(fill = okabe_ito[["blue"]], alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Cumulative advantage (squared incidents)")








Figure 2: Cumulative loss differential, months 31–48: running sum of benchmark minus VendorScore squared error (squared incidents). Above zero favours VendorScore.






How to read the plot. Each month we ask which forecast was closer. The line is the running total, rising when VendorScore wins and falling when the 12-month average wins.
What the plot tells you. The line ends 22.3 above zero, with 4.1 accumulated by month 36 and 18.2 after it. It climbs unevenly, with several losing months, so this is a mixed record with a favourable tilt, not a steady edge.



Show the code
tab <- data.frame(
  Window = c("Months 31–48 (n = 18)", "Months 37–48 (n = 12)"),

How to read the table. Each row is a stretch of months. The MAE columns show the average miss in incidents per month; the MSE columns square each miss, so large misses count more. The last two columns test whether the accuracy gap is bigger than expected if both forecasts were equally good.
What the table tells you. VendorScore has lower errors in both windows. The p-value is the chance of a loss difference at least this extreme if expected accuracy were equal and the test’s assumptions held; 0.235 and 0.309 are not small. That means no detectable advantage here, not proof of equality.

VendorScore’s MSE is 22% lower over the full window and 20% lower after the shift, while its MAE advantage nearly vanishes after the shift (2.03 versus 2.08). The vendor’s claimed AUC of 0.81 comes from its own development data. It cannot show whether VendorScore stays reliable at this bank once conditions change. Only the bank’s own ongoing monitoring can (§VII).

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text:
So What?
On this evidence VendorScore gets the level of incidents closer than the simple benchmark does, but the advantage is statistically unproven and concentrated in a period when the benchmark lagged a rising trend. The comparison covers aggregate counts, not vendor rankings.
The April 17, 2026 interagency Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) lists out-of-sample and out-of-time testing under model testing (§IV), and benchmarking and ongoing monitoring under validation (§V). The cumulative-differential chart fits there: a line a committee can watch. This is partial validation: it tests outputs, not the method.

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text:
Actionable Insights
Sound practice suggests benchmarking every vendor model against a named simple alternative, out of sample and out of time, and adding the loss differential to ongoing monitoring so that deterioration triggers review.

title: Question 2: Does It Beat a Simple Model?
text:
Footnotes


forecastdom 0.1.0, dm_test() with h = 1, squared-error loss, two-sided alternative, Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold correction (reference distribution t with n − 1 degrees of freedom), benchmark errors first. At h = 1 the package’s variance is the sample variance of the loss differences divided by n, with no autocorrelation adjustment.↩︎

title: Reproducibility
text: Every number on this site is computed from synthetic data generated by R/simulate.R from seed 34, with every analysis choice set in params.yaml. Nothing is downloaded during a render, so rendering the same commit with the same package versions gives the same results. This page explains how to rebuild the site, records the environment it was built in, and states where the results can mislead.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Quick start
The code and data are in the GitHub repository patrick-lefler/three-questions-for-any-risk-model. To rebuild everything from a clean copy:
git clone https://github.com/patrick-lefler/three-questions-for-any-risk-model
cd three-questions-for-any-risk-model
Rscript -e 'renv::restore()'   # once: install the package versions pinned in renv.lock
Rscript run_all.R
The rendered site is written to docs/. run_all.R runs the scripts in the Pipeline table in order, stops at the first failure, clears the Quarto freeze cache, calls quarto render, then runs the word count and the page tests. To re-render the pages from the artifacts already in data/ without rerunning the analysis, run quarto render instead.

How to read the table  Each row is a setting that shapes the results. The last column says whether it is an analyst’s assumption, a standard convention, or a feature planted in the synthetic data.
What the table tells you  Most settings are assumptions. Changing the windows, risk bands or deletion budget would change the reported numbers, so each is recorded in one place.
Every random stream is seeded explicitly. R/simulate.R calls set.seed() with the SIM_SEED value (default 34); R/fit_models.R, R/analysis_calibration.R and R/analysis_fragility.R each call set.seed(par_get("seed")) at the top. The xgboost model is trained with nthread = 1, and no step runs in parallel, so results do not depend on the number of cores. The seed sweep on page 4 reruns the generator with seeds 1 to 40 in temporary folders and never touches data/.






Noteparams.yaml





# Single register of every analysis parameter, read by the R scripts (R/params.R).
# basis: "assumption" = a choice made by the analyst; "convention" = a standard
# default; "planted" = a deliberate feature of the synthetic design.
# range: values over which a sensitivity check would be reasonable (not all were run).
# The simulator's own parameters live in R/simulate.R (validated; not edited here);
# they are listed under `simulator` for reference only and are NOT read from this file.

seed:
  value: 34
  basis: "assumption: selected during development from seeds 1-40 (26 of 40 pass the generator's checks)"
  range: "1-40 (seed sweep on page 4)"

windows:
  classifier_train: {value: [1, 30],  basis: "assumption: vendor's training months",  range: "fixed by the generator's train/test split"}
  calibration_fit:  {value: [31, 36], basis: "assumption: six months, out of sample for the classifier", range: "3-12 months"}
  overlay_eval:     {value: [37, 48], basis: "assumption: all months remaining after the calibration window", range: "set by calibration_fit"}
  forecast_eval:    {value: [31, 48], basis: "assumption: all months after classifier training", range: "fixed"}

vendorscore:
  sharpen:           {value: 1.5,  basis: "planted: overconfidence, logit scaled around the training base rate", range: "1.0-2.0"}
  xgb_eta:           {value: 0.05, basis: "assumption: the vendor's hidden choice",  range: "0.02-0.2"}
  xgb_max_depth:     {value: 3,    basis: "assumption: the vendor's hidden choice",  range: "2-6"}
  xgb_min_child_weight: {value: 5, basis: "assumption: the vendor's hidden choice",  range: "1-20"}
  xgb_subsample:     {value: 0.8,  basis: "assumption: the vendor's hidden choice",  range: "0.5-1"}
  xgb_colsample:     {value: 0.8,  basis: "assumption: the vendor's hidden choice",  range: "0.5-1"}
  xgb_nrounds:       {value: 150,  basis: "assumption: the vendor's hidden choice",  range: "50-500"}

calibration:
  ece_bins:        {value: 10,   basis: "convention", range: "5-20"}
  bootstrap_draws: {value: 1000, basis: "convention: vendor-history resamples", range: "500-5000"}
  band_low_upper:    {value: 0.01, basis: "assumption: illustrative Low/Medium boundary (monthly incident probability)", range: "0.005-0.02"}

title: Reproducibility
text:
Caching

Analysis artifacts (data/*.rds, data/*.csv). The pipeline scripts write them; the pages only read them. They are committed to git, so quarto render on a fresh clone works without rerunning the analysis. Nothing invalidates them automatically: after editing a script or params.yaml, run Rscript run_all.R to rebuild them.
Quarto freeze (_freeze/). _quarto.yml sets freeze: auto, so a full quarto render re-executes a page only when that page’s .qmd file changes. Edits to the R/ scripts or to the artifacts in data/ do not count as a change. run_all.R deletes _freeze/ before rendering for this reason. After changing anything else, render each page explicitly (for example quarto render index.qmd), because Quarto always executes a page that is rendered on its own. _freeze/ is not in git.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Known limitations

Limits of reproducibility

Bit-for-bit equality is expected only on the same platform and package versions. Floating-point and BLAS differences across machines can change low-order digits.
The three testing packages (probcal 0.2.0, forecastdom 0.1.0, falsifyr 1.0.0) are young CRAN releases whose defaults may change between versions; renv::restore() installs the pinned versions from the CRAN archive. The VendorScore scores depend on the xgboost version.
Quarto versions affect rendering, not the numbers.



Model limitations

Synthetic data. Confounding, regime shift and overconfidence are planted. Real use needs NorthPoint’s vendor-month panel, incident definition and dated SOC 2 reports.
Few events. 75 evaluation incidents and 18 forecast months limit power; more history could change pages 2 and 3.
Thin overlay window. Six months and 28 incidents is little. A real overlay needs a refit schedule and tolerances set in advance.
Information timing. Start-of-month availability of patch latency and financial health is assumed; real feeds need timestamps.
One dataset. Seed 34 was chosen in development; the seed sweep on page 4 checks repeatability only.
Partial validation. Scores and outcomes only; the vendor’s internals stay unseen.

The results show how the three questions can be put to a black-box score using only its outputs and the bank’s own outcomes. They are not evidence about any real vendor model. Treat the numbers as an illustration of the method, and rerun the analysis on real data before drawing conclusions about a specific model.
